passage:
Dear Yamini Didi,

You asked me to write when things felt heavy. They do.

Yesterday Kiran texted "ok" when I asked about cricket on Sunday. Just "ok." I've read it maybe twenty times. It must mean he's fed up with me. And in the chemistry test I got 14 out of 25, which proves I'm hopeless at everything. When I try to think of anything I've done right this year, my head goes blank.

It's been like this for weeks, not days. I don't know if "ok" really means anything. Maybe it only feels true because I feel low.

Mummy noticed I've gone quiet at dinner. She's asked the school counsellor to see me on Thursday. I said I'd go.

Write back soon.
Ramesh

qa.q: What did Kiran text when Ramesh asked about cricket?
qa.a: Just "ok."

qa.q: Why does Ramesh read 'ok' as a sign Kiran is fed up?
qa.a: Weeks of low mood make everything look like rejection and failure, so a plain reply feels like proof, even though Ramesh half suspects the mood is shaping it.

qa.q: What is a wise next step, and who is already helping?
qa.a: Seeing the school counsellor on Thursday, as Mummy arranged, and keeping Yamini Didi in the loop; weeks of low mood deserve that kind of care.

qa.q: How might Kiran have meant that text?
qa.a: Kiran may simply have been busy or agreeing to Sunday; the short reply could be completely neutral.

grounding: A teenager in a weeks-long low mood reads a neutral text as rejection and recalls only failures, while a parent arranges counsellor support.

passage:
Madhuri, don't laugh, okay? The group chat went quiet after I posted my painting. Two hours, nothing. I just know everyone thinks it's bad. Then Sir wrote "Vandana, see me after class" on my essay, and I'm sure it's because it's terrible. Everything I've done this term has flopped. The debate, the maths quiz, all of it.
You say Sir only wanted to talk about the art competition? Maybe. I don't know. My brain keeps saying it's bad news.
It's been weeks, honestly. I wake up already tired, and things I loved feel grey.
You think I should tell someone? My Chachi is easy to talk to. And the counsellor has that open hour on Fridays.
Okay. If you come with me on Friday, I'll go.

qa.q: What did Sir write on Vandana's essay?
qa.a: "Vandana, see me after class."

qa.q: Why is Vandana so sure the quiet group chat means the painting is bad?
qa.a: Weeks of low mood make silence and neutral notes feel like rejection, and the mind serves up only past flops as evidence.

qa.q: What plan does Vandana agree to, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Going to the counsellor's Friday open hour with Madhuri and perhaps talking to Chachi; weeks of feeling grey deserve care from trusted adults.

qa.q: How might Madhuri see the quiet group chat?
qa.a: Madhuri probably thinks people were just busy, and may be worried that Vandana has felt low for so long.

grounding: A teenager tells a friend how silence and a teacher's note feel like rejection during weeks of low mood, then agrees to seek adult help.

passage:
Kunal used to be the loudest one in the dressing room. This month he's different, and I'm not sure what's going on inside him.
On Tuesday Coach posted the team list with Kunal as substitute. Most of us are subs sometimes. Kunal read it and said, "Coach has given up on me." Then he listed every missed goal since June, like he'd kept a diary of them.
When I texted him "see you at practice", he replied, "Why, so you can laugh?" I wasn't laughing. I just meant see you.
I'm Samir, just his mate, not a doctor. But this has gone on for weeks. So I told Coach quietly after practice. Coach thanked me, said they'd call Kunal's parents that evening, and asked me to keep being a friend.

qa.q: What did Kunal reply when Samir texted 'see you at practice'?
qa.a: "Why, so you can laugh?"

qa.q: Why does being a substitute feel like proof to Kunal that Coach has given up?
qa.a: His low mood makes a normal team decision read as rejection and pulls up every missed goal as evidence, so the judgment feels like fact.

qa.q: Was Samir right to tell Coach? Why?
qa.a: Yes; the low mood had lasted weeks, and a caring adult can involve Kunal's parents and get proper help, while Samir keeps being a friend.

qa.q: What is it like for Samir to get that text?
qa.a: Samir feels misread, having only meant see you, and worried about how different Kunal has become.

grounding: A teammate notices a teenager reading neutral messages as rejection and recalling only failures for weeks, and tells a caring adult.

passage:
Tuesday: Suraj, fifteen, texted Wasim a long message about the cricket trials. Wasim replied: "ok." Suraj stared at it. He's sick of me, he thought. Lying on his bed, he went through a list in his head: failed the physics test, dropped the catch in August, said something dumb in class. Nothing good came to mind.
The next Monday: The class group was planning a birthday outing and nobody tagged him. Suraj decided they didn't want him there. He skipped dinner again. His mother noticed his plate untouched for the third time that week.
Thursday: His mother sat on his bed. "You've been far away for weeks, beta. Talk to me?" After a long silence he said, "Everyone's tired of me." She didn't argue; she listened, then said, "We'll see the school counsellor together tomorrow, and the doctor too." That evening Wasim knocked. "Why didn't you reply? I was waiting."

qa.q: What was Wasim's reply to Suraj's long message?
qa.a: "ok."

qa.q: Why did "ok" feel like proof to Suraj that Wasim was sick of him?
qa.a: In his low mood, a neutral reply felt like rejection, and his mind only brought up his failures, so the gloomy reading seemed like plain fact.

qa.q: What choice did Suraj's mother make that mattered most?
qa.a: She noticed the pattern over weeks, sat with him and listened without arguing, and arranged for them to see the school counsellor and a doctor together.

qa.q: How does Wasim's visit show the gap between Suraj's view and what others felt?
qa.a: Wasim had been waiting for a reply, not avoiding Suraj, which shows the rejection Suraj felt came from his mood, not from his friend.

grounding: Over several days a teenager's low mood makes neutral messages feel like rejection and brings up only failures, until a caring adult steps in with professional help.

passage: Bhavna, you've been quiet all week, so let your Nani tell you about the year I was fifteen. A grey fog settled on me that winter. My friend Raunak sent a short letter from Pune, just three lines, and I read it as, she's done with me. I remembered every wrong answer I'd ever given, every time I'd been laughed at, and nothing else. It all felt like plain truth, not a mood. My teacher, Mrs D'Souza, noticed I'd stopped eating lunch. She didn't brush it aside. She spoke to my parents that same week, and my father took me to our family doctor, who listened for a long time and helped us find proper care. Years later Raunak told me she'd written in a rush before her exams. So, Bhavna, if a fog like that sits on you for long, you tell me. We'll get help together.

qa.q: How many lines was Raunak's letter from Pune?
qa.a: Just three lines.

qa.q: Why did Nani read Raunak's short letter as rejection?
qa.a: Her low mood made neutral things feel like proof that people were done with her, and her mind kept serving up only past failures.

qa.q: What choices by the adults around Nani made the difference?
qa.a: Mrs D'Souza noticed and spoke to her parents, and her father took her to the family doctor, who helped them find proper care.

qa.q: How might Raunak have felt learning, years later, how that letter had been read?
qa.a: Raunak would likely be sad and surprised, since the short letter was only written in a rush before exams, not meant as rejection.

grounding: An elder recalls how a low mood as a teen made a neutral letter feel like rejection, and how caring adults and a doctor helped.

passage: So, Kalyani, you want Tanvir's honest version of class eleven. For about two months I was low, like a grey filter on everything. A friend would text "ok" and I'd read it as "go away." Someone didn't save me a seat, and I decided the whole class was done with me. If you'd asked about my year, I'd have listed every test I bombed and not one good thing. And it felt like fact. That's the scary part. It didn't feel like a mood, it felt like seeing clearly. My Ammi noticed I'd stopped eating with the family. One evening she sat on my bed and asked straight out how long I'd been feeling like this. The next day we went to the school counsellor together, and then to a doctor. Slowly, "ok" went back to meaning ok.

qa.q: How long did Tanvir say the low period in class eleven lasted?
qa.a: For about two months.

qa.q: Why did reading "ok" as "go away" feel so true to Tanvir at the time?
qa.a: The low mood made everything look rejecting and hopeless, and Tanvir felt sad and alone, so the gloomy reading felt like seeing clearly rather than like a feeling.

qa.q: What did Ammi do well, and what could a friend do in a similar situation?
qa.a: Ammi asked directly how long it had been going on and took the next step to the counsellor and a doctor; a friend could tell a trusted adult rather than keep quiet.

qa.q: How might the friend who texted "ok" have seen that message?
qa.a: The friend probably meant nothing more than ok, and may have felt confused or hurt if Tanvir pulled away because of it.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose low mood turned neutral messages into rejection and only failures into memory, and an adult who got caring professional help.

passage:
Monday. Sudha texted Rekha before school: "Can't walk with you today." Rekha stared at the screen. She's tired of me, she thought, like everyone. On the bus she replayed every bad mark she'd got that term and couldn't think of one good one.
Thursday. Rekha had eaten lunch alone for four days, head on the desk. Her class teacher, Mrs Pillai, kept her back after the bell. "You've seemed very down for a while, Rekha. I'm worried about you." Rekha's eyes filled. That afternoon Mrs Pillai called Rekha's parents and walked her to the school counsellor, who met all three of them before the day ended.
Two weeks later. After a few talks with the counsellor, Rekha scrolled back to Monday's message. Underneath it was a second one she'd skipped: "Dentist, ugh. Save me a seat at lunch?" She still had grey days. But she could see this one differently now.

qa.q: What did Sudha's Monday text say?
qa.a: "Can't walk with you today."

qa.q: Why did Rekha believe Sudha was tired of her?
qa.a: Rekha was in a low, lonely mood, so the plain message felt like rejection and only her failures came to mind, making the gloomy reading feel like fact.

qa.q: Which of Mrs Pillai's steps mattered most, and why?
qa.a: She named her worry kindly, called Rekha's parents the same day and took her to the counsellor, instead of waiting to see if it passed.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel if she learned Rekha had read her text as rejection?
qa.a: Sudha would likely feel surprised and sorry, since she only had a dentist visit and was even asking Rekha to save her a seat.

grounding: Shows a teenager in a low mood reading a neutral message as rejection and recalling only failures, and adults giving caring professional help.

passage: Jeevan, you think nobody understands being sixteen and miserable? Your Damini atya does. When I was fifteen, in Kolhapur, I went through a long grey time. My best friend didn't wave to me across the market once, and I decided she hated me. I wrote a list in my notebook of every mistake I'd made since class five. Every page felt like proof. My aunt, the one who lived with us, noticed I'd stopped singing while I cleaned rice. She didn't say "cheer up." She asked how many weeks it had been, and I said I didn't know, many. The very next morning she took me to our family doctor, who sent me to speak with someone trained in this. It took months. My friend, it turned out, had forgotten her glasses that day.

qa.q: Why hadn't Damini's friend waved to her in the market?
qa.a: Her friend had forgotten her glasses that day.

qa.q: Why did the list of mistakes feel like proof to young Damini?
qa.a: She was in a long low mood, sad and hopeless, which made her recall only failures and made those gloomy judgments feel like facts.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why was it a wise choice?
qa.a: Her aunt asked how long it had been and took her to the doctor the next morning, which brought in trained help instead of just telling her to cheer up.

qa.q: How might the aunt have felt noticing Damini had stopped singing?
qa.a: The aunt likely felt worried and caring, since a small change in a daily habit told her something was wrong.

grounding: Illustrates, through an elder's memory, a teenager's low mood turning a neutral moment into rejection, and an adult seeking professional help.

passage:
Vasudha, sixteen, had been feeling low for weeks. The school's WiFi was down, and she was trying to finish her project on her phone in the library. Her friend Omkar texted: "Can't make it to study group today."

Vasudha read it and felt a sinking in her chest. He doesn't want to be around me, she thought. Like the time I messed up the debate. And the time I failed chemistry. She could suddenly remember every failure, one after another.

The school librarian noticed her sitting with her head in her hands and sat down beside her. "Rough day?"

Vasudha nodded. The librarian listened, then said, "When we feel low for a long time, everything looks darker. Can I walk you to the counsellor now?" Vasudha hesitated, then nodded.

qa.q: What did Omkar's text say?
qa.a: "Can't make it to study group today."

qa.q: Why did Vasudha read Omkar's text as rejection?
qa.a: Her low mood made the neutral message feel like proof nobody wanted her, and it brought back memories of failures.

qa.q: What did the librarian do that helped?
qa.a: The librarian noticed, sat with her, listened, and walked her to the counsellor right away.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel if he knew how his text was read?
qa.a: Omkar would likely feel surprised and sorry, since he probably just couldn't make it.

grounding: A teenager in a low mood reads a neutral message as rejection and recalls only failures, and a caring adult steps in.

passage:
Hafsa, fifteen, sat in her room in Hyderabad, scrolling through the class group. Nobody had replied to her message about the project. She read it as: nobody cares.

She'd been feeling this way for a while. She kept remembering the bad times: the dance performance where she tripped, the friend who stopped calling. It felt like facts, not feelings.

Her uncle Zubin, visiting for the week, knocked on her door. "You've been quiet for days. Can I sit?"

Hafsa shrugged. He sat and waited. Slowly she told him.

"That sounds really heavy," he said. "Feeling low for this long isn't something you should carry alone. Let's tell your mum tonight, and find someone good you can talk to." Hafsa nodded, eyes wet.

qa.q: Who knocked on Hafsa's door?
qa.a: Her uncle Zubin, visiting for the week.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa read the silence in the class group as "nobody cares"?
qa.a: Her long low mood made neutral silence feel like rejection and pulled up memories of failures, which felt like facts.

qa.q: What did Zubin do that was helpful?
qa.a: He sat and listened, took her feelings seriously, and planned to tell her mum that night and find a professional to talk to.

qa.q: How might Hafsa's classmates see the unanswered message?
qa.a: They may not have noticed it or were busy, not meaning any rejection at all.

grounding: A teenager in a low mood reads neutral silence as rejection and recalls only failures; a caring adult steps in.

passage:
"Kashish, you haven't eaten dinner with us all week."

"Not hungry, Papa."

"Raghav told me you left the cricket group."

"They don't want me. Nobody ever replies to me."

"Raghav said they asked where you were."

"He's just saying that."

"Beta, you've been this low for a while now. Everything looks dark when you feel this way. It doesn't mean it's true."

"It feels true."

"I know. That's why I'm worried. I've booked a time with Dr Mehta for Saturday. I'll come with you. And tonight, can we just sit together?"

Kashish looked at the floor for a long time. "Okay."

qa.q: When did Papa book a time with Dr Mehta?
qa.a: For Saturday.

qa.q: Why does Kashish think the cricket group doesn't want her?
qa.a: Her low mood makes neutral things feel like rejection, so even Raghav's news seems false to her.

qa.q: What did Papa do well?
qa.a: He named the low mood kindly, didn't argue about facts, booked a professional appointment and offered to stay with Kashish that night.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel if he heard Kashish thinks he's just saying things?
qa.a: Raghav might feel hurt or worried, since he was trying to reach out.

grounding: A teenager in a low mood reads neutral messages as rejection; a caring parent responds and seeks professional help.

passage: Last term I went through weeks when everything looked grey. My friend Urmila would text "ok" and I'd read it as "I'm sick of you." A teacher said "see me after class" and I spent the whole period sure I was in trouble; she only wanted me for the quiz team. When I tried to think about the year, I remembered only failures: the maths paper, the missed goal, the day I cried on the bus. It all felt like plain fact, not a mood. My mother noticed I'd stopped eating breakfast and asked, "Swati, how long has it felt like this?" I said, "Weeks." That same evening she booked a time with the school counsellor. Talking helped me see the mood was painting everything. It still comes back sometimes, but now I tell someone.

qa.q: What did the teacher actually want after class?
qa.a: She wanted Swati for the quiz team.

qa.q: Why did Swati read Urmila's "ok" as "I'm sick of you"?
qa.a: Swati had been in a low, heavy mood for weeks, and that sadness turned neutral messages into rejection and made the judgment feel like plain fact.

qa.q: What made a difference, and what should someone in Swati's place do if the mood returns?
qa.a: Swati's mother noticed, asked, and booked the school counsellor that same evening; if it returns, telling a trusted adult or the counsellor early helps.

qa.q: How might Urmila have experienced those weeks?
qa.a: Urmila may have felt confused and hurt, sending ordinary "ok" texts without knowing they were being read as rejection.

grounding: A teenager in a low mood reads neutral messages as rejection and recalls only failures, and a parent arranges counselling support.

passage: Class teacher's note, Friday. For about three weeks Dilnaz has seemed low: head down, homework half done. Today Damini passed her a note about lunch, and Dilnaz read it and said, "She doesn't want me there." The note said, "Sitting by the tap today?" When I asked Dilnaz how the term had gone, she listed only mistakes and said it was "just a fact" that she was bad at everything. I told her I was glad she had talked to me, and that low moods can make things look darker than they are. With her agreement, I rang her father this afternoon, and I have booked her with the school counsellor for Monday morning. I will check in with her again before she leaves today.

qa.q: What did Damini's note actually say?
qa.a: "Sitting by the tap today?"

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz read the lunch note as rejection?
qa.a: She has felt low for about three weeks, and that heavy mood made a friendly note look like rejection and her mistakes look like fact.

qa.q: Which of the teacher's steps matter most?
qa.a: Listening without dismissing, explaining that low moods darken things, ringing her father that day, booking the counsellor, and checking in before she leaves.

qa.q: What is it like for Damini when her friendly note is taken badly?
qa.a: Damini may feel confused and hurt, since she meant to invite Dilnaz to lunch.

grounding: A teenager in a low mood reads a friendly note as rejection, and a teacher arranges caring adult and professional help.

passage:
Wednesday.
Nilesh didn't reply to my message about the project for five hours. Obviously he thinks I'm useless. Then Ma'am returned our essays and I only saw the red marks, not the "good ideas" at the top. At dinner I tried to list anything good from this month and couldn't. It's been like this for weeks, like grey glass over everything.
Later: Nilesh finally replied: "sorry, phone died, your part's great." So I was wrong about him. That scared me more, honestly: how sure I felt. I showed this page to Mumma. She held my hand and said we'll see the school counsellor together, and she'll ring the doctor tomorrow too. I feel a bit lighter just telling her.
Shreya

qa.q: What was Nilesh's reply?
qa.a: "Sorry, phone died, your part's great."

qa.q: Why did Shreya feel so sure that Nilesh thought Shreya was useless?
qa.a: A low mood lasting weeks, like grey glass over everything, made the silence feel like rejection; how certain it felt scared Shreya once the real reply came.

qa.q: What did Shreya do that was wise?
qa.a: Showed the diary page to Mumma, who planned to see the school counsellor together and ring the doctor; a low mood that lasts needs caring adults and professional help.

qa.q: How might Mumma feel reading the page?
qa.a: She is likely worried and tender, holding Shreya's hand, and glad to have been told.

grounding: A teenager in a long low mood misreads a delayed reply as rejection and turns to a parent for support.
